paragraphs.text: Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism characterized by malonic aciduria, developmental delay, seizure disorder, hypoglycemia, and cardiomyopathy (Wightman et al., 2003). Other reported features include mild mental retardation, hypotonia, vomiting, and metabolic acidosis (Gao et al., 1999). Sacksteder et al. (1999) described it as a lethal disorder characterized by cardiomyopathy and developmental delay, with phenotypes reminiscent of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation disorders.

paragraphs.text: Brown et al. (1984) described a patient with deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme malonyl-CoA decarboxylase, an inborn error of metabolism not recognized previously. The enzyme defect was first suspected because of persistent excretion of malonic and methylmalonic acids in the urine in a child with repeated episodes of vomiting, some requiring hospitalization. Disturbances of lipid metabolism were demonstrated.

paragraphs.text: Haan et al. (1986) reported a second child with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, a boy who was mildly mentally retarded and presented with vomiting, a seizure, hypoglycemia, and mild metabolic acidosis during a urinary tract infection. His urine contained increased amounts of malonic, methylmalonic, succinic, adipic, glutaric, and suberic acids. Mitochondrial malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity in cultured fibroblast extracts was 4% of the mean control value.

paragraphs.text: By RT-PCR analysis of fibroblast RNA from 2 previously reported consanguineous Scottish patients with malonyl-CoA decarboxylase deficiency, FitzPatrick et al. (1999) identified 2 different homozygous truncating mutations in the MCD (MLYCD) gene: a 442C-G transversion resulting in a premature stop codon (S148X) in the N-terminal half of the protein, and an intronic mutation (IVS4-14A-G) generating a novel splice acceptor sequence that resulted in a 13-bp insertion in the mature RNA, causing a frameshift with predicted protein truncation. Both mutations segregated appropriately within the families and were not found in 100 normal unrelated individuals, which confirmed the cloned transcript as the human MCD ortholog.

paragraphs.text: By genomic sequencing of the MLYCD gene in 9 unrelated patients with MLYCD deficiency, Wightman et al. (2003) identified 16 of 18 pathogenic alleles. Western blot analysis of patient fibroblasts (from 8 of these patients and 2 previously reported patients with homozygous mutations) using C-terminal antisera showed that the 66-kDa band was absent in 6 patients and substantially reduced in 3; 1 patient showed increased protein with a smeary 68- to 83-kDa band. Mutations studied for subcellular localization included an extreme N-terminal mutation (c.8G-A; G3D), a 25-base deletion between the putative mitochondrial and peroxisomal initiating codons (M1 and M40), and a point mutation ablating the second of these (c.119T-C; M40T).

paragraphs.text: Sacksteder et al. (1999) found that the MCD protein carries a canonical type-1 peroxisomal targeting signal (SKL), that recombinant MCD had high intrinsic malonyl-CoA decarboxylase activity, and that MCD resides in both the cytoplasm and peroxisomes.
